message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) belong to very different branches of the mammalian tree:

| Taxonomic level | Lion | Zebra |
|-----------------|------|-------|
| Class | Mammalia | Mammalia |
| Sub‑class | Theria | Theria |
| Infraclass | Eutheria (placentals) | Eutheria |
| Super‑order | Laurasiatheria | Laurasiatheria |
| Order | Carnivora (Feliformia) | Perissodactyla |
| Family | Felidae | Equidae |

Because they diverge at the order level, their most recent common ancestor is the last common ancestor of the two orders **Carnivora** and **Perissodactyla**. That ancestor lived in the late Cretaceous to early Paleogene, roughly **70–80 million years ago**, and was a small, generalized mammal that gave rise to the entire Laurasiatherian clade.

So, the common ancestor of a lion and a zebra is a **Laurasiatherian mammal that lived about 70–80 million years ago**, the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor in the mammalian lineage. Both are mammals, but lions are felids (family Felidae), zebras are equids (family Equidae). They diverged from a common ancestor in the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla. Actually, lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). So their common ancestor would be a more distant mammalian ancestor, perhaps a placental mammal ancestor. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the eutherian ancestor. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species: that would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both orders, which is the clade of Laurasiatheria? Actually, Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of the clade Laurasiatheria. The last common ancestor of Carnivora and Perissodactyla would be the ancestor of the Laurasiatheria. So the common ancestor would be a mammal from the late Cretaceous or early Paleogene. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is older. But the question likely expects: "The common ancestor of lion and zebra is a mammal from the Laurasiatheria clade, dating back to about 70-80 million years ago." Or "the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which lived around 70 million years ago." Or "the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is a mammal that lived around 70 million years ago, belonging to the clade Laurasiatheria." Alternatively, they might want "the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla." So answer accordingly.

We don't need to call any function. Just answer.
